title: Growth isn't required
hook: some people report growth after trauma and some don't, and no one owes a silver lining

segments.voice: Yesterday: pain, and the clench we add around pain. Your line was soften around it. Did one ache loosen, even a little, when you stopped bracing? Day seven hundred thirty-seven.

A card arrives after a hard year. On the front, in curly gold letters: everything happens for a reason. Someone meant it kindly. Still, a line like that can land like homework. Find the reason. Write up the lesson. Show your growth by Friday. Two psychologists studied what happens to people after terrible events, and what they found is more honest than the card. Some people do grow. Some don't. And today's lesson is the part the card leaves out: growth isn't required.
screen: `EVERYTHING HAPPENS FOR A REASON.` → `IT CAN LAND LIKE HOMEWORK.` → `GROWTH ISN'T REQUIRED.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Richard Tedeschi and Lawrence Calhoun, psychologists who studied people after trauma, gave one pattern a name: posttraumatic growth. Some of the people they studied described changes on the far side of the struggle. Closer relationships. New priorities. A sense of their own strength. A deeper spiritual life. Second, the fine print, and it matters. In their account, the growth comes out of the struggle with what happened, not out of the event itself. The disaster isn't the teacher. And growth and distress can sit side by side: a person can report real growth and still hurt. Third, not everyone reports it. Their work describes growth as something some people find, not a stage everyone reaches, and not a test anyone passes or fails. Nobody owes the world a silver lining. Fourth, an old text that makes room for this. Earlier this year we read Psalm thirteen, a complaint that turns toward trust by its last verse. Psalm eighty-eight doesn't turn. It's a prayer from the bottom, and its last line in the King James Bible is this: "Lover and friend hast thou put far from me, and mine acquaintance into darkness." That's where it stops. No lesson, no bright side. And it sits in the Bible of Jews and Christians alike, ending and all. Some readers take comfort in exactly that: a holy book that lets a sufferer end in the dark without being told to cheer up. Growth may come, quietly, later on. Or it may not. Either way, the hard thing doesn't have to earn its keep.
screen: `A NAME: POSTTRAUMATIC GROWTH.` · `IT COMES FROM THE STRUGGLE, NOT THE EVENT.` · `NOT EVERYONE REPORTS IT.` · `PSALM 88 ENDS IN THE DARK.` · then, large: `GROWTH ISN'T REQUIRED.`

segments.voice: Settle, and let the breath find its own pace. Bring to mind one hard thing, past or present. Not the hardest; just one. Notice whether the mind rushes to ask what it taught you. Let that question sit down. For these two minutes, the hard thing doesn't have to mean anything. It happened. It hurt. That's enough to say. If you pray, you can offer it with no moral attached. If a lesson shows up on its own, let it come. Just don't go digging for one. The bell holds the time.
Posttraumatic growth, the pattern Tedeschi and Calhoun named in some survivors of trauma: closer relationships, new priorities, a sense of their own strength. Today's word.
Your line: that sounds hard. Today, if someone tells you about a hard time, skip the silver lining. Just say, that sounds hard, and leave it there. Day seven hundred thirty-seven.

howItsDone: Psychologists who study posttraumatic growth describe it as something some people report after a struggle, not a requirement; Jews and Christians keep Psalm 88, a prayer that ends in darkness, in their scriptures.

trapdoor: what you thought: every hard thing comes with a lesson, and finding it is your job.
what it means: some people report growth after hard things and some don't. neither is a failure.
what a scholar hears: Tedeschi and Calhoun's posttraumatic growth, which comes from the struggle, not the event, and can sit alongside distress; and Psalm 88, which ends in darkness.

notes: Audit (2026-10-01): Psalm 88:18 KJV checked exact; Psalm 13 callback matches day 713; Tedeschi and Calhoun summary (growth from the struggle, coexists with distress, not universal) is fair. No change.

Index hook says 'many report growth after trauma'; the claims rule keeps the script to 'some people', since no count or proportion is cited. The meta keeps the index line; the script's hook line is softened to match.

Tedeschi and Calhoun paraphrased: growth arises from the struggle with the aftermath, not from the trauma itself; growth and distress can coexist; the five domains (relating to others, new possibilities, personal strength, spiritual change, appreciation of life) are given in part. Confirm the summary is fair.
Psalm 88:18 KJV quoted; the claim that Psalm 88 does not turn toward trust and ends in darkness is a reading of the text. Psalm 13 (day 713) cited as a psalm that turns to trust at verse 5.
'Show your growth by Friday' is a light joke on the listener's life, not on any belief.
